extractions.value: At presentation, she fulfilled clinical criteria for SPS (1, 2). She did not have Babinski signs. Supportive evidence for this diagnosis was the absence of lumbar lordosis in plain radiographs of the spine early in the course, the collapse of L4 and L2 vertebrae (thought to have been the result of lumbar paraspinal muscle spasms), and the presence of chronic inflammatory cells in the pancreas (some associated with islets) consistent with a reaction to anti-islet cell antibodies.

extractions.value: A video recording of a third typical spell with simultaneous polygraph monitoring showed that it began with disrupted regular breathing and increased muscular activity in the internal hamstrings and abdominal muscles... Repetitive firing of muscles then increased in amplitude and frequency and spread to cervical paraspinal and all the scalp muscles. Only a few muscles were sampled for the polygraph recording. When the spell was fully developed, most muscles were involved (see video). In the early part of the spell, muscles fired synchronously at a rate of -2-3 Hz. This rate then increased to 9 Hz, and breathing stopped.

extractions.value: The patient had an unusually long course of encephalomyelitis whose presenting clinical features resembled those of SPS. Autopsy showed diffuse encephalomyelitis. The patient had cardiorespiratory arrest and died. The lack of testing for anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies is a recognized limitation.
